Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data
through Recursive Self-Improvement

Piccolo Team†
Abstract

We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that co-evolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories.11 1 Decision-Index-Vision snapshot: 2026-11-17 18:35:34 UTC, with 86 entrants. Full-score is the equal-weight mean of Public and Private. Size-specific ranks use nominal total-parameter classes Decision Index Contributors [2026]. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family’s development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency — earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B–9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.

1 Introduction

While generative models excel at open-ended synthesis, real-world autonomous systems bottleneck on decisions, such as selecting actions, enforcing guardrails, and routing workflows under strict latency and reliability constraints. A decision model maps a supplied state, question, and candidate set to probabilities over answers or actions Kirkby et al. [2026], Dhankhar et al. [2026], Zhuang et al. [2026]. We present Piccolo, which implements this Jev-like interface for text and images through direct candidate-logit readout from a language-model head. Its System-1-style predictions support Choice over alternatives, Score on ordered levels, and Noul for yes/no judgments. Callers can select actions, threshold confidence, or escalate decisions using the returned distribution; Appendix B gives the formulation.

Piccolo powers four core application domains (Figure 2): (a) General decisions: visual interpretation, document checks, and routing for enterprise workflows with locally retained sensitive data. (b) Low-latency interaction like games: repeated perception–action decisions support movement and combat in Zenless Zone Zero, jump timing in Mario, and merge choices in 2048 Piccolo Team [2026]. (c) Agent harnesses: tool review, permissions, and context management in systems built with AgentScope Gao et al. [2025]; QwenPaw integrates Piccolo for tool review and context compaction AgentScope Team [2026]. (d) Data processing: filtering, operator selection, and quality judgments within Data-Juicer workflows Chen et al. [2023]. HarnessJevBench and DataJevBench organize recurring harness and data decisions into complementary evaluation suites HarnessJevBench Contributors [2026], DataJevBench Contributors [2026].

Spanning five sizes from 0.8B to 27B, Piccolo establishes a new Pareto frontier on Decision Index Vision (Figure 6). Piccolo-27B ranks #1 overall (75.59 Full, 70.97 Private); 9B and 4B lead their Private parameter classes (65.04 and 63.49). The 0.8B and 2B models score 55.17 and 66.64 Public, respectively. Piccolo-27B also ranks among the leading models on HarnessJevBench HarnessJevBench Contributors [2026] (84.41) and DataJevBench DataJevBench Contributors [2026] (82.60).

Agentic Data Engineering drives Piccolo’s RSI. Training dynamics and fine-grained data buckets characterize where the model learns reliably, where progress stalls, and which capabilities compete. Linking these responses to domain, supervision, and task structure turns an aggregate score into a map of capability boundaries. Agents use this map to propose data changes, build experiments, and carry the resulting knowledge into the next research decision Ding et al. [2026]. Researchers interactively guide objectives and introduce methods while agents automatically revise mixtures, synthesis targets, and training choices. Shared assets preserve discoveries and lessons throughout evolving progress.

Across ∼\sim600 experimental runs (approximately 2.8×10212.8\times 10^{21} FLOPs at the hardware’s peak BF16 performance)22 2 Estimated from approximately 6,300 PPU-ZW810E accelerator-hours using a reference BF16 peak rate of 123 TFLOP/s per device. Hardware references and accounting assumptions are detailed in Appendix E., our agent-led loop uncovered development dynamics that challenge standard post-training heuristics: (1) Data granularity dictates capability trade-offs: Fine-grained filtering sharpens agentic workflow decisions, whereas broader adaptive mixtures favor general text reasoning (Section 4.2). (2) Recipes and backbones must be co-selected: Identical data mixtures unlock divergent strengths across different model generations (Figure 9). (3) Failed branches hold latent value: Even regressive runs yield reusable parameter update directions and diagnostic signals that accelerate subsequent iterations (Section 5). These observations connect the RSI design to the family-level results and the experiments behind them. In summary, our main contributions are threefold:

  • •

    A multimodal decision model family: competitive size–quality trade-offs, leading Vision Full and size-specific Private results, and applications from enterprise workflows to interactive control.

  • •

    A data-driven RSI methodology: fine-grained feedback, explicit proposals, and reusable experiments turn model development into a continuing agent-led research loop.

  • •

    Empirical insights for decision model development: systematic findings connect supervision, validation coverage, synthesis, backbone selection, and post-training to concrete experimental outcomes.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Decision Model

The decision model maps a state, a question, and an ordered candidate set to a probability distribution. A training example is (s,u,C,q)(s,u,C,q), where ss contains text, images, or structured observations, uu specifies the question, C=(c1,…,cK)C=(c_{1},\ldots,c_{K}) lists the candidates, and qq is their target distribution. The three interfaces share this representation: Choice compares supplied alternatives, Noul uses a yes/no pair, and Score uses ordered rating levels.

Piccolo combines a visual encoder, a connector, and a language backbone with its native language-model head. The backbone uses bidirectional attention over the prompt in full-attention blocks. In hybrid backbones, linear-attention blocks retain their original causal computation. To construct the input x=compile⁡(s,u,C)x=\operatorname{compile}(s,u,C), each candidate ckc_{k} is assigned a single-token label τ⁡(k)\tau(k) and presented with its description. Images are encoded by the visual encoder and passed through the connector to the language backbone alongside the text input. An optional sidecar OCR model supplies extracted text as an additional image-associated observation.

At the answer position, the backbone produces a hidden state hθ​(x)h_{\theta}(x). The native language-model head projects this state to vocabulary logits through WLMW_{\mathrm{LM}}. Piccolo reads the logit for each candidate label τ⁡(k)\tau(k) and applies a softmax over these KK logits to obtain the decision distribution:

zθ,k​(x)=[WLM​hθ​(x)]τ⁡(k),pθ,k​(x)=exp⁡zθ,k​(x)∑j=1Kexp⁡zθ,j​(x).z_{\theta,k}(x)=\bigl[W_{\mathrm{LM}}h_{\theta}(x)\bigr]_{\tau(k)},\qquad p_{\theta,k}(x)=\frac{\exp z_{\theta,k}(x)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp z_{\theta,j}(x)}. (1)

Appendix B details input organization and the supervision–error relationship.

2.2 Training and Optimization

Supervised training minimizes cross-entropy over the candidate distribution for both hard and soft targets:

ℓCE(q,pθ)=−∑k=1Kqklogpθ,k,ℓCE−H(q)=DKL(q∥pθ).\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}(q,p_{\theta})=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{k}\log p_{\theta,k},\qquad\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}-H(q)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p_{\theta}). (2)

For a one-hot target, the loss is the negative log-probability of the correct answer. For soft targets, subtracting target entropy separates distributional mismatch from uncertainty in the supervision. Cross-entropy is a proper scoring rule, providing a basis for calibration-oriented supervision Zhang [2004]. Accuracy additionally records whether the correct candidate ranks first. Section 3 uses these complementary signals to guide data changes.

We use candidate-level reinforcement learning to refine decision accuracy in models after supervised training. These continuations optimize the candidate distribution with correctness-based, group-relative updates and supervised replay.

We use weight-space optimization to search for improved decision accuracy by directly modifying the trained model parameters. Candidate weights are constructed by interpolating checkpoints, rescaling parameter projections, or applying directions extracted from previous training updates Akiba et al. [2025]. This allows us to explore combinations and adjustments of learned parameters without running a new gradient-based training stage for each candidate. Appendix C summarizes more details of RL objective and these refinement methods.

2.3 Data Sources and Preparation

To support generalization across domains, task structures, and input modalities, we collect a broad range of text and visual decision data. The collection spans everyday decisions, computing and technology, mathematics and science, humanities, and arts. Existing sources and synthesized tasks cover reasoning, retrieval, preference judgments, visual interpretation, and action selection. Appendix C.1 provides the source inventory.

Training on these heterogeneous sources requires preserving the evidence and conditions that justify each target while making their supervision consistent with the shared decision interface. Conversion places each question in the (s,u,C,q)(s,u,C,q) format, retaining action preconditions, relevance distinctions, image–answer alignment, and the original supervision distribution. Data-Juicer supports normalization, filtering, and auditing Chen et al. [2023]. We remove duplicates to limit redundant training exposure. Task-specific audits repair or exclude incomplete and incorrect data that would otherwise introduce misleading supervision. To extend coverage, we use CuES for data synthesis Mai et al. [2025].

The resulting pool shown in Figure 3 contains 663K examples, comprising 311K text and 352K image–text decisions. Appendix C details the data composition. We annotate examples by domain, capability, task function, difficulty, and learning value. These labels group examples into semantic slices whose training dynamics and decision accuracy can be analyzed together. Each example retains its identity and source, allowing agents to trace slice-level findings back to the underlying data for inspection, revision, or targeted synthesis. Section 3 describes this feedback loop, and Appendix C.3 provides the annotation scheme.

3 Recursive Self-Improvement with Data-driven Agents

In conventional model development, failed training runs are discarded as sunk compute costs. In Piccolo’s RSI process, we capture and organize every successful or regressive experiment as structured epistemic capital. By binding fine-grained semantic slices, training dynamics, and weight-space trajectories into a persistent research memory, our agent orchestrator transforms brute-force hyperparameter search into cumulative scientific discovery.

3.1 Evolving Objective and Iteration Loop

Evolving objective.

We seek to improve Piccolo’s decision performance through experiments on data strategies and model configurations. Let Sdev​(m,𝒱)S_{\mathrm{dev}}(m;\mathcal{V}) measure performance on the candidate-based tasks defined in Section 2.1, using a held-out development set 𝒱\mathcal{V} for each research phase. The objective is

maxψ1:TSdev(mTbest;𝒱)subject to∑t=1Tct≤B,\max_{\psi_{1:T}}\;S_{\mathrm{dev}}\bigl(m_{T}^{\mathrm{best}};\mathcal{V}\bigr)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}\leq B, (3)

where ψt\psi_{t} is an experimental proposal and mTbestm_{T}^{\mathrm{best}} is the best evaluated model, including the starting model, after TT experiments. The number of allocated accelerators and the exploration window define BB in accelerator-hours; ctc_{t} is the execution and evaluation cost of experiment tt in the same units. Each proposal specifies a starting model, a data strategy, and permitted training or inference changes. Data strategies determine source selection, mixtures, revisions, and synthesis. Models are compared under a common scoring rule, with independent confirmation assessing transfer (Section 3.2).

Atomic iteration loop.

Figure 4 organizes the cycle as proposal, build and experiment, results, and diagnosis. Let ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} record the available models, annotated data assets, completed comparisons, research memory, and remaining budget. Agents use this state to turn findings into subsequent experiments Ding et al. [2026]:

ℛt−1→Proposeψt→Experiment(mt,𝐟t,ct)→Diagnose & Updateℛt.\mathcal{R}_{t-1}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Propose}}\psi_{t}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Experiment}}(m_{t},\mathbf{f}_{t},c_{t})\xrightarrow{\text{Diagnose \& Update}}\mathcal{R}_{t}. (4)

Feedback 𝐟t\mathbf{f}_{t} summarizes learning dynamics, inference results, and data statistics by semantic slice. Diagnosis connects gains and regressions to these slices and the tested settings. The update records resulting assets and findings in shared research memory and revises proposal priorities. For example, a mastered synthetic slice can prompt harder variants. Human researchers can optionally introduce new directions, set exploration priorities and budgets. Subsequent proposals can start from any retained model and reuse findings across historical branches.

3.2 Orchestrator Design around the Loop

Running the atomic loop requires coordinating feedback, data and model assets, execution, and human guidance. We organize these functions into an orchestrator, maintaining ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} through versioned records of experiment lineage and proposal priorities across concurrent branches (Figure 4).

Structured Feedback.

Semantic labels align training dynamics, inference outcomes, and data statistics by source, supervision, and candidate count. Hard-target cross-entropy tracks the probability assigned to the correct candidate Tewari and Bartlett [2007], Zhang [2004]; for soft targets, subtracting target entropy yields target–prediction KL (Appendix B). Loss trajectories describe how the predicted distribution evolves, while repeated inference tracks repaired and newly missed decisions. Aggregating these signals by semantic slice reveals differences in learning progress among examples with shared domain and capability tags. The agent links these observations to sample records to identify coverage gaps, uneven learning, and label conflicts. These findings guide the data actions in Figure 4: downsampling redundant examples, rebalancing mixtures, revising conflicting labels, and synthesizing examples for underrepresented capabilities.

Persistent Assets and Research Memory.

To preserve experimental context, we link proposals, data, models, configurations, protocols, and results. We apply DataJuicer-Panel to manage these records within ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t}. Standardized records support cross-branch retrieval; lineage tracks model ancestry and reused recipes or findings. Memory associates gains and regressions with slices and settings, guiding experiments from other starting models.

Composable Experiment Execution.

To execute a proposal, we compose data, training, inference, and evaluation steps. We use DataJuicer-Sandbox Chen et al. [2025]: Factories provide these capabilities, Hooks bind assets and settings, and Pipelines sequence steps. These interfaces combine the data operations in Figure 4 under the settings in Table 2; analysis and execution proceed concurrently.

Validation and Comparison.

Development comparisons track improvements and retained skills; disjoint confirmation sets and broad evaluations assess transfer. Source and construction identities organize splits, while semantic labels expose coverage. Audits check sample validity, input versions, and evaluation completeness. Outcomes and execution costs return to the shared research state (Appendix D.4).

Proposal Selection and Human Steering.

Agents rank proposals by expected improvement, retained skills, information value, and cost, recording their target, parent, action, and comparator. Short diagnostics resolve uncertainty; longer runs develop promising directions. Human researchers set priorities, review major changes, and introduce new methods and data sources to be explored. The human-preference and agent-accumulated findings collectively determine the next experiments.

3.3 Instantiation in Piccolo Development

We instantiated the orchestrator with a retained model, an indexed data pool, a development protocol, and a compute allocation. Training runs returned models, predictions, measured cost, and findings for subsequent proposals. Figure 5 traces an effective data-rebalancing iteration from actual Piccolo training, showing how the assets, execution, and memory components in Section 3.2 support successive proposals.

(1) Execute a retrieval proposal. P1 combined replay with a retrieved supplement to train M1 from retained model M0. (2) Diagnose the regression. Arts performance fell from 55.19 to 52.66; joining these predictions to the selected-data records showed an arts share of 3.1% among training questions. Diagnosis K1 made arts coverage the focus of the next experiment. The asset records preserved the selected groups, configuration, and parent model alongside this finding.

(3) Revise the mixture and compare. P2 tested knowledge-only and balanced knowledge–arts supplements from the same M0, with shared replay groups, learning rate, and seed. Complete-group selection preserved native supervision: recipe shares count groups, tag shares count questions, and group composition determines question and token totals. Under the common development protocol, balanced model M3 outscored M2 by 0.30 points overall and 0.70 on arts. Memory K2 retained this comparison and the remaining arts gap to M0 for subsequent proposals. Model lineage records the shared parent; research lineage carries the diagnosis from P1 into P2 and its findings back into ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t}.

4 Performance and Model–Data Co-Evolution

Post-training is traditionally treated as optimizing a dynamic model over a static data recipe. Piccolo reframes data-model development as a coupled dynamical system: as the model’s capability boundary shifts, the optimal data distribution and recipe must shift with it. A recipe that accelerates learning in an early checkpoint or on one backbone generation can induce regressions in another.

4.1 Overall Performance

Decision Index.

Piccolo-27B ranks first on Vision Full (75.59) and Private (70.97), with 80.22 Public (Table 3a). Its Public profile exceeds JDI-Decision V1 by 1.78 points on CV-Bench, 4.02 on BLINK, and 3.38 on MMMU-Pro Vision; Appendix D.3 gives all eleven tasks. Piccolo-9B and 4B score 65.04 and 63.49 on Private, while 2B and 0.8B score 66.64 and 55.17 on Public.

Application evaluations.

HarnessJevBench covers tool use, permissions, memory, and execution; DataJevBench covers filtering, processing plans, and output quality; JevBench covers general decisions. Piccolo-27B scores 84.41 on Harness, 82.60 on Data, and 92.21 on JevBench, outperforming the strongest external Harness baseline by 1.36 points in the completed batch. Piccolo-9B and 4B score 71.53/66.10 on Harness and 72.40/70.20 on Data, exceeding both size-matched D3 and Valen models. Their Private Vision scores also exceed both baselines. Appendix D.2 gives the full comparison.

4.2 Data Evolution

Data evolution involves coverage (D1), allocation (D2), and joint recipes (D3).

D1 Feedback-guided data revision restores coverage.

Held-out feedback and semantic labels identify gaps for targeted replacement: replacing 10% of an early recipe outperforms matched random replacement by 2.11 development points (56.56 vs. 54.45). Later, restoring underrepresented preference coverage raised the arts/preference component from 48.91 to 53.42. For sparse slices, proposals specify automated collection with deduplication and sensitive-information removal, or model-guided synthesis from verified seeds. The model’s pass rates on the new tasks—63.43% for state tracking and 15.38% for budget allocation—then identified where difficult examples remained.

D2 Training dynamics guide adaptive data allocation.

The Structured Feedback interface in Section 3.2 supplies target–prediction KL and changes in decision correctness on held-out questions. These readouts guide Filter & Rebalance in Figure 4: rebalancing revises bucket shares as learning progresses, while filtering selects examples using source-level loss and verification outcomes. Figure 8 aligns the resulting allocations with each branch’s scores. Rebalancing elevated Public Text to 67.93, versus 67.36 for the fixed recipe. Adding filtering reached 84.58 Harness and 82.20 Data, with Text at 66.98.

D3 Joint recipes consolidate gains from data evolution.

Joint decision training combined general decisions, image-dependent tasks, and workflow additions, with replay material for established skills. OCR-aware SFT aligned supervision with image-associated text available at inference. At one consolidation node, a Qwen3.6-27B descendant improved from 71.89 to 79.59 on Vision, 68.64 to 81.36 on Harness, and 73.20 to 81.40 on Data (Figure 9a). Crucially, newer backbones do not guarantee across-the-board superiority under a fixed recipe (Figure 9b). Trained on the exact same data order, the earlier Qwen3.5 initialization (79.97) outperformed both Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8 on Vision (79.59 and 77.86), whereas Qwen3.8 dominated agentic Harness tasks (85.93), versus 80.85 and 81.36 for Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6. Model initialization and data recipes must therefore be co-adapted to match target deployment priorities.

4.3 Model Evolution

Model proposals reused these data assets to compare training strategies (M1), model composition and refinement (M2), and inference (M3), linking each choice to its measured capability response.

M1 Training choices benefit from matched supervision.

Bidirectional attention benefited from matched training and inference: Text development scores reached 69.01, versus 68.20 with causal attention and 68.14 when only inference became bidirectional. Staged SFT and RL paired broad supervision with targeted adaptation. Full-parameter and low-rank continuations tested how broadly to update the model. OCR-aware SFT established the input–decision correspondence before candidate-level RL and supervised replay addressed residual errors. Objective and data weighting then evolved together: from a shared parent and the same examples, fixed-weight GRPO reached 77.13 Public Vision, candidate CE 77.31, and confidence/progress-weighted GRPO 77.35. These results made both the supervision format and the distribution of learning weight part of the training proposal.

M2 Model composition integrates complementary capabilities.

Cross-modal merging combined branches strengthened by different data recipes. In one exploration, retaining the visual modules of an image–text model and blending its language parameters with a text-oriented branch boosted Public Text from 67.89 to 68.15 while trading off Vision from 77.29 to 75.70 (Table 4a). The mixture retained part of each branch’s advantage. Candidate-distribution integration explored a complementary route inspired by MOPD Ma et al. [2026]. Reference predictions supplement the original targets on selected examples. Exact matching reached 82.80 Data, versus 82.20 for the original-target continuation, while Harness stayed at 84.92 and Vision remained near 77.07 (Table 4b). These branches provide distinct task profiles for subsequent composition.

Weight-space editing refined candidate combinations through module scaling and low-rank update directions Akiba et al. [2025]. One selected configuration combined (i) approximately 5% stronger visual attention projections in blocks 9–17, (ii) slight attenuation of feed-forward outputs in language layers 8–23, (iii) log-decay offsets in selected late gated-attention blocks, and (iv) rank-8 updates to output projections in layers 30–31. The combined model elevated Public Vision to 70.75 (vs. 70.10 for the retained reference), with a 0.68-point Harness decrease. Earlier, merging five data-specialized descendants boosted Public Text to 63.11, surpassing the strongest individual branch at 62.78.

M3 Input organization and layer reuse offer distinct inference gains.

Context evolving changed question previews, repeated context, and aggregation across candidate-label views (Figure 10a). Adaptive rereading reached 68.56 Public Text at 1.02×\times input volume. Full rereading scored 68.64; two- and three-view aggregation reached 68.69 and 68.71 at 1.90×\times and 2.08×\times input volume.

Recurrent inference reused layer ranges within the forward pass (Figure 10b). Two half-step passes over each of two adjacent ranges raised Text development scores from 69.15 to 69.75 and Harness from 80.85 to 87.12. Reusing a single range yielded 69.58 on Text, whereas reducing the two-range step to one quarter lowered the score to 67.41. A separate recurrent configuration raised 2B Public Vision from 65.85 to 66.64.

5 Discussion

5.1 Optimizing Single Benchmarks Masks Cross-Task Regressions

Isolated gains in one capability often mask severe regressions in another, even without weight updates. Merely reorganizing the input layout at fixed weights boosted Public Text by +1.14 points while causing a 3.00-point drop on DataJevBench (Figure 11a). Semantic slices locate the affected capabilities; held-out task and source groups assess their transfer (Section 3.2). This profile identifies the skills to preserve or strengthen in subsequent data revisions.

5.2 More Compute on Fixed Data Degrades Generalization

Scaling training exposures on a static data pool skews the capability balance rather than uniformly improving the model. Over 1M sample exposures on a fixed pool, Data scores crept up by ++0.60, but Text and Harness degraded significantly by −-1.29 and −-1.69 points (Figure 11b). This demonstrates that dynamic data curation is more compute-efficient than prolonged static training. In addition, the diverging trajectories motivate comparing longer training with revised coverage and allocation. Proposals from a shared retained model make these alternatives directly comparable.

Inference introduces another allocation choice. Adaptive rereading achieved 68.56 Public Text; three-view aggregation further reached 68.71 with 2.04×\times the input tokens of adaptive rereading. Structural changes were similarly sensitive to their setting: two-band half-step recurrence gained 0.60 Text development points, whereas quarter-step recurrence lost 1.74 (Figure 10). Head- and channel-level rescaling also entered the search; strong visual-branch attenuation failed to improve the retained development score. The useful computation depends on both the task and the current model.

5.3 Capability Integration and Research Reuse

Combining specialized branches changes which capabilities survive. The cross-modal merge in Table 4a gained 0.26 Public Text points over its image–text parent while losing 1.59 Vision points. Candidate-distribution matching produced a smaller redistribution: Data improved by 0.60 over training on the original targets, with Harness unchanged and Vision nearly unchanged (Table 4b). Branch selection can use complementary task strengths, with the retained gains measured after integration.

Even “failed” training runs contain actionable gradient signals. In one notable lineage, a continuation branch regressed below its parent on the development set; however, extracting specific components of its parameter update and applying them with a negative coefficient yielded a winning weight-space merge. This underscores the value of preserving full experimental lineage: by connecting parent checkpoints, parameter deltas, and slice-level responses, the orchestrator converts apparent dead-ends into composable building blocks for future iterations (Appendix D.5).

5.4 Relation to Prior Work

Decision-model research explores complementary training and inference choices. Mammoth and Elephant combine data recipes and bidirectional attention Kirkby et al. [2026]; Drex studies supervised and reinforcement learning Dhankhar et al. [2026]; StartLux adds confidence-guided deliberation Zhuang et al. [2026]. Evolutionary merging and MOPD study capability integration Akiba et al. [2025], Ma et al. [2026]. Agentic Data Engineering Ding et al. [2026] and open-ended self-improvement Zhang et al. [2026] guide research through feedback and accumulated discoveries. Piccolo connects these ideas through candidate-level feedback, evolving data recipes, and reusable model branches.

6 Conclusion and Future Directions

Piccolo demonstrates that advancing frontier decision models requires more than scaling parameters or static datasets; it requires scaling the research loop itself. Through Agentic Data Engineering, Piccolo co-evolves data curricula and model weights across a 0.8B to 27B family, establishing state-of-the-art performance across visual judgment, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive control.

Beyond the released weights, our development campaign exposes fundamental dynamics of post-training: surrogate loss optimization frequently decouples from discrete decision accuracy, static data pools inevitably induce cross-capability interference, and optimal data recipes are strictly contingent on backbone initialization. By embedding these diagnostics into an autonomous, memory-backed orchestration loop, we shift post-training from manual trial-and-error to systematic, self-correcting engineering.

Looking forward, the convergence of fast System-1 decision models and deliberative System-2 reasoning points toward hybrid cognitive architectures. Future work will extend this recursive co-evolution to adaptive test-time deliberation, multi-turn environmental interaction, and automated synthesis for long-tail capability frontiers; ultimately advancing not just the models that make decisions, but the autonomous systems that build them.

Appendix B Candidate Supervision and Input Organization

B.1 Supervision and Decision Error

Section 2.1 defines the shared decision format and candidate readout in Equation 1. Equation 2 gives the supervised objective and its decomposition into target entropy and distributional mismatch. Here we relate this loss to decision error and detail the input implementation.

For hard-target decisions, loss also supplies a simple bound on the error indicator. With natural logarithms and y^=arg⁡maxk⁡pθ,k\hat{y}=\arg\max_{k}p_{\theta,k}, an incorrect prediction implies pθ,y≤1/2p_{\theta,y}\leq 1/2, hence

𝟏[y^≠y]≤−log⁡pθ,ylog⁡2.\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}\neq y]\leq\frac{-\log p_{\theta,y}}{\log 2}. (5)

Averaging gives the same bound on empirical error by mean candidate loss divided by log⁡2\log 2. At the population level, expected cross-entropy equals conditional target entropy plus expected KL to the true conditional distribution; minimizing the latter recovers the Bayes decision rule Tewari and Bartlett [2007], Zhang [2004]. In finite experiments, mean loss tracks probability changes across examples while accuracy tracks which candidates cross the decision boundary. Reporting both retains the graded training response and the operational answer changes, as in Table 1.

Hard-target correctness and target probability accompany this distributional measure. Slice comparisons retain supervision form, candidate count, source, and semantic labels. A repeated fixed-question measurement retains its input and target, while a training-window summary follows the examples encountered in that window.

Candidate scoring uses the native language-model head at the readout position. The compiler maps option order to the tokenizer’s valid candidate labels, checks the mapping, and stores the target distribution separately from the visible prompt. Packed examples retain isolated boundaries. Bidirectional prompt masks apply to full-attention blocks; linear-attention blocks retain their original causal computation in the hybrid backbones.

Context evolving studies question-list prefixes, focused-question presentation, and length-aware layouts. Multimodal inputs preserve image order and question-to-image alignment. OCR text is supplied as an image-associated observation alongside the original image. A fixed recognizer prepares the training cache; evaluation extracts text from the input image using the corresponding preparation policy.

Appendix C Data Sources and Training Overview

C.1 Source Inventory

The initial text inventory contains 6.65M records and 8.93M questions from 43 source collections. A record can contain several questions. Table 5 lists all 43 collections, grouped here by their primary use. Source conversion retains the original supervision and associates each question with its parent record. The visual inventory shown in Figure 3 includes SAT-v2, Geo170K, TallyQA, NLVR2, TQA, and ArxivQA, covering spatial relations, geometry, counting, visual reasoning, diagrams, and scientific figures.

C.2 Data Composition

Training curricula combine general text decisions, visual tasks, targeted synthesis, and replay of established skills. Figure 3 shows a joint-pool snapshot of 663K examples: 311K text and 352K image–text decisions. Representative curricula draw on approximately 380K or 700K examples, with different balances of visual material and text coverage. Source and task-form metadata support sampling while preserving the original supervision distributions. Held-out feedback guides subsequent additions and allocation changes, as described in Section 4.2.

C.3 Annotation Taxonomy and Semantic Buckets

The annotation schema separates the subject of a decision from its required capability, task function, input quality, and estimated learning demands. Table 6 lists its 13 axes and 551 selectable values. Domain has 334 leaf categories under 26 parent groups; capability has 144 leaf labels under 14 parent groups. The 40 parent groups organize the hierarchy, while the three native response interfaces—Choice, Noul, and Score—are stored separately as task-format metadata. Multiple labels can apply on axes such as decision basis or challenge factors.

Annotations describe the input and requested decision. Supervision targets and measured outcomes remain separate fields joined by example identity. This supports comparisons within a domain, across capabilities, or under a fixed supervision form.

The semantic view in Figure 3 covers approximately 210K annotated examples. Its 26 domain groups are summarized into everyday life (54.7%), computing and technology (13.6%), mathematics and science (12.7%), humanities, arts, and society (5.8%), and other domains (13.2%). Choice, Noul, and Score account for roughly 59%, 25%, and 16%; difficulty levels 2–3 account for about 77%. These views describe the coverage available to feedback-guided selection.

C.4 Training and Refinement Objectives

Supervised stages optimize candidate cross-entropy using BF16 training, Adam, and a learning-rate schedule with warmup and decay. Proposals vary the data allocation and the trainable language, connector, and visual components. The comparisons in Figure 9 evaluate how a shared recipe interacts with backbone initialization.

Candidate-level reinforcement learning samples actions from the current candidate distribution and assigns correctness rewards. Group-normalized advantages AgA_{g} guide the update, together with supervised anchoring and a frozen-reference distribution:

ℓtarget=−1G∑g=1Gstopgrad(Ag)logpθ(ag)+λℓCE+βDKL(pθ∥pref).\ell_{\mathrm{target}}=-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\operatorname{stopgrad}(A_{g})\log p_{\theta}(a_{g})+\lambda\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}+\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\theta}\|p_{\mathrm{ref}}). (6)

Here GG is the number of sampled candidate actions, and λ\lambda and β\beta control the supervised and reference terms. Supervised replay accompanies targeted updates. Weight-space proposals explore checkpoint interpolation, module rescaling, and low-rank update directions; held-out comparisons assess the resulting task profiles.

Appendix D Evaluation Details and Supporting Results

D.1 Evaluation Metrics and Protocols

For Public Vision, let sjs_{j} denote the benchmark’s chance-adjusted score on task jj and ωj\omega_{j} its relative weight. The aggregate is

SPublic=∑jωj​sj∑jωj.S_{\mathrm{Public}}=\frac{\sum_{j}\omega_{j}s_{j}}{\sum_{j}\omega_{j}}. (7)

The nine core tasks have unit weight; R-Bench-M and MMMU-Pro Vision have relative weights 0.5 and 0.25. Full is the equal-weight mean of Public and Private. All official Vision results use the snapshot specified in the opening footnote 1. Appendix A gives the expanded Full rankings; Table 7 summarizes Piccolo’s score components.

D.2 Application Comparisons

The application evaluations cover the hard-target subset of HarnessJevBench v0.5 (295 tasks, 303 questions), 500 DataJevBench questions, and 231 JevBench questions. Table 8 extends the main comparison to all evaluated baselines. Each external model uses its published input format, classification head, attention mechanism, and temperature, together with the official scoring scripts. Figure 13 illustrates the full Harness and Data capability sets.

D.3 Public Vision Task Profiles

Table 9 reports all eleven Public task scores. The first group follows the six leading Full-score entries; the remaining groups compare smaller models. Piccolo-27B exceeds JDI-Decision V1 by 1.78 points on CV-Bench, 4.02 on BLINK, and 3.38 on MMMU-Pro Vision, as highlighted in Section 4.1.

D.4 Development Feedback and Validation

The data-allocation study uses about 4,000 tuning questions and 2,000 disjoint confirmation questions. The tuning set supports repeated allocation decisions; confirmation readouts assess transfer to other questions before broad benchmark evaluation. Source, group, and construction identifiers define split membership and keep related variants together. Fixed-question readouts retain their inputs and targets, while training-window summaries describe the examples encountered during training.

The branches in Figure 8 have comparable sample-exposure budgets. Their recorded trajectories include differences in starting parameter states and concurrent changes to several data allocations. The displayed outcomes characterize those complete research paths. On the 341 fixed workflow questions in Table 1, target–prediction KL and net correctness changes jointly inform the subsequent mixture update.

D.5 Selected Comparison Protocols

The joint-training comparison in Figure 9a holds input and inference adaptation fixed, including the prompt attention mask and image-associated OCR. The backbone comparison in panel (b) uses a shared recipe and data order. The attention comparison in Section 4.3 uses the same Text development questions across mask combinations; the objective comparison starts from a shared model with the same examples and update budget.

For synthesized tasks, quality verification checks the target, while model pass rate measures current difficulty (Table 10). Family identifiers keep related constructions together when splitting examples. These measurements guide seed revision and the admission of further synthesized data.

The input-transfer comparisons in Figure 11a preserve model weights within each pair. Panel (b) follows eleven checkpoints on a fixed pool through 1.024 million sample exposures, counting repeated presentations. The archive also retains unsuccessful continuations and their parameter differences; selected update components can be reused in later combinations, as discussed in Section 5.

Appendix E Compute Accounting

The archived 27B campaign comprises 647 training attempts and approximately 6,300 accelerator-hours on Alibaba PPU Zhenwu 810E devices (PPU-ZW810E) Alibaba Cloud [2026]. Accelerator-hours sum occupied devices multiplied by training duration across attempts. This accounting covers the archived 27B training campaign; subsequent multimodal and smaller-model training, evaluation, synthesis, and candidate-search workloads are recorded separately.

To estimate peak-equivalent compute, we use a reference BF16 rate of pref=123p_{\mathrm{ref}}=123 TFLOP/s per device.33 3 The reference rate is listed in the ZW810E specification table of a publicly reposted presentation. It is the throughput assumption for this estimate. For H≈6,300H\approx 6{,}300 accelerator-hours,

Cpeak=H×3,600×pref×1012≃2.8×1021​FLOP,C_{\mathrm{peak}}=H\times 3{,}600\times p_{\mathrm{ref}}\times 10^{12}\simeq 2.8\times 10^{21}\ \text{FLOP}, (8)

corresponding to approximately 32 PFLOP/s-days. This estimate expresses accelerator time at the reference peak rate; executed FLOPs depend on achieved throughput. The training volumes in Appendix C describe individual curricula, while this compute total aggregates the exploration attempts.

Training scales in related work.

Table 11 summarizes reported training scales for decision models. Piccolo’s representative multimodal curricula use approximately 380K or 700K examples (Appendix C), supporting iterative refinement with fewer than one million examples per recipe.
